title: A unified framework for scalable differential testing for spatial omics - Nature Biotechnology
text:
Download PDF

AbstractA key challenge in spatial omics is identifying features whose values vary depending on both cell type and the surrounding cellular niche. Existing methods designed for spatial transcriptomic data do not generalize well to modalities beyond count-based data and do not scale efficiently to current data volumes. Here we introduce spotGLM, a mixture-aware generalized linear modeling framework for cell-type-specific differential testing across spatial modalities, and SPARROW, a power-preserving data distillation strategy for scalable inference. SpotGLM accommodates diverse data types including count-based gene expression, binomial isoform proportions and continuous chromatin accessibility scores within a unified statistical framework. We demonstrate the framework across spatial omics applications. On Visium HD data of colorectal cancer and mouse kidney, we recover cell-type-specific niche effects with serial-slice cross-platform validation. On long-read spatial RNA-seq data, we resolve cell-type-specific isoform switching in the mouse olfactory bulb. On spatial ATAC-seq data from mouse brain, we recover cell-type-specific spatial variation in regulatory motif accessibility.

MainSpatial barcoding technologies have transformed molecular profiling by enabling high-resolution, multimodal mapping of the chromatin state, transcriptome, RNA splicing and protein abundance within intact tissue. Advances such as Slide-seq1, Stereo-seq2, high-definition spatial transcriptomics3 and Visium HD now achieve subcellular resolution, while platforms such as spatial ATAC-seq4 and long-read spatial sequencing5 extend spatial profiling beyond gene expression. These technologies allow the study of how molecular programs vary across tissue microenvironments. However, the rapid increase in spatial resolution and multimodality has created statistical challenges that existing analytical frameworks are not designed to address.A central task in spatial omics is identifying molecular features whose variation depends jointly on cell type and local spatial context. In spatial barcoding technologies, each coordinate typically contains mixtures of multiple cell types. Consequently, cell-type-specific responses to local spatial environment must be inferred from aggregated spot-level measurements. While deconvolution methods estimate cell type proportions, they do not provide a statistical framework for testing cell-type-specific niche effects. Existing approaches for spatial differential expression, such as C-SIDE6 and NicheDE7, are primarily tailored to count-based RNA data and assume specific distributional forms. These methods do not generalize naturally to other spatial modalities, such as isoform proportions from long-read sequencing or motif accessibility scores from spatial ATAC-seq. Moreover, their computational cost becomes prohibitive at the scale of current high-resolution datasets.Therefore, two conceptual challenges arise. The first is mixture confounding; spot-level measurements represent weighted aggregates across cell types and naive analyses that assign each spot to a dominant cell type or perform region-level stratification can inflate false discoveries or obscure true cell-type-specific effects. The second is scalability; as spatial datasets approach millions of coordinates, full-resolution statistical modeling becomes computationally impractical without sacrificing statistical power.To address these challenges, we introduce two complementary innovations. First, we develop SpotGLM, a mixture-aware generalized linear model (GLM) framework for cell-type-specific differential testing across spatial modalities. SpotGLM extends the classical GLM by explicitly modeling spot-level observations as mixtures of cell-type-specific exponential-family distributions. This formulation accommodates diverse data types, including count-based gene expression, binomial isoform proportions and approximately Gaussian chromatin accessibility scores, within a unified statistical framework. By deriving the likelihood, gradient and Fisher information for the mixture model, SpotGLM enables calibrated hypothesis testing of cell-type-specific niche effects from spot-level data.Second, we introduce SPARROW (scalable power-adaptive reduction for representative omics workflows), a power-preserving data distillation strategy that enables bounded-runtime inference. SPARROW leverages optimal design principles and greedy subset selection to select spatial coordinates that retain power for downstream inference. Unlike heuristic downsampling, geometric sketching8 or rasterization9, SPARROW explicitly optimizes a power-based objective tied to the downstream model, allowing bounded-runtime inference even as dataset size increases. The name SPARROW comes from the idiom ‘a sparrow may be small but it is fully formed with all vital organs’.Together, SpotGLM and SPARROW form a unified framework for scalable, mixture-aware spatial differential testing.We demonstrate the breadth and necessity of this framework across four distinct spatial omics applications. In Visium HD colorectal cancer (CRC), we perform serial-slice cross-platform validation against single-cell-resolved Xenium data, demonstrating accurate recovery of cell-type-specific niche programs from spot-level mixtures. In mouse kidney, we model a continuous physiological osmolarity gradient and uncover spatially structured fibroblast transcriptional programs not captured by anatomical region labels alone. In spatial long-read transcriptomics of the olfactory bulb, we provide a cell-type-resolved analysis of spatial isoform switching, formally distinguishing within-cell-type splicing changes from confounding effects of gene expression and cell composition. Lastly, in spatial ATAC-seq of mouse brain, we enable mixture-aware, cell-type-specific inference of regulatory motif accessibility, extending spatial modeling beyond RNA to chromatin regulation.ResultsSpotGLM: a general framework for cell-type-specific differential testing across spatial modalitiesWe first describe SpotGLM for identifying cell type-specific niche differential signals in compositional spatially barcoded data. Although our model is for measurements taken at the spot level, to motivate the model, we first considered the setting where we observe individual cells in space. Focusing on one feature at a time, let Yi be the readout of the given feature for cell i. For example, to model RNA expression Yi would be the count of a gene, to model isoform switching Yi would be the isoform-specific read counts and to model chromatin accessibility Yi would be the summarized activity (that is, total normalized accessibility) of a gene or motif (Fig. 1a). Let Ti be the cell type of cell i, which we assume is given. Our goal would be to test the cell-type-specific spatial niche dependency of the feature, where spatial niche would be encoded by a n × p design matrix X, where n is the number of cells and p is the dimension of the spatial niche encoding.Fig. 1: Overview of the SpotGLM framework and SPARROW data reduction strategy.Full size imagea, SpotGLM enables cell-type-specific differential testing in spatial omics data by modeling measurements at the spot level as a mixture of cell-type-resolved GLMs. The model accommodates diverse data types by specifying an appropriate link function: log for counts (for example, gene expression), logit for proportions (for example, splicing) and identity for continuous data (for example, motif or gene activity scores in ATAC-seq). b, SPARROW is a power-preserving data reduction method that greedily selects an informative subset for downstream differential testing. c, SPARROW constructs the subset iteratively, adding the data point that most reduces an A-optimal trace-inverse Fisher information criterion.In this hypothetical single-cell scenario, to allow flexibility for different data modalities, we would use a GLM that assumes that the conditional expectation of Y given X is linear after transformation F(⋅). F is called the link function of the GLM. Let Xi be the ith row of X (a 1 × p vector); then, we would have$$F\left(E\left[{{Y}_{i}|X}_{i}\right]\right)={X}_{i}{\beta }_{{T}_{i}},$$
(1)
where the p × 1 coefficient vector β would depend on cell type Ti. Our goal would be to estimate, for each spatial covariate j and each cell type t, the cell-type-specific coefficient βt,j that quantifies the relationship between the covariate and the feature. We would further like to distinguish those niche covariates and cell types for which βt,j are nonzero.The choice of the link function F would depend on data modality. If the readout Y were approximately normal, such as in the case of ATAC motif or gene activity scores, then the natural link function corresponding to the normal distribution would be the identity function. For alternative splicing analysis, where Y|X would be binomial, the natural choice for F would be the logit function. For count-based data, the natural choice for F corresponding to Poisson or negative binomial regression would be the log function (Fig. 1a).However, in spatial barcoding technologies, instead of individual cells, we observe spots with predefined spatial coordinates. Thus, instead of observing Yi directly, we observe spot-level readouts Zs, where each spot s is allowed to contain a mixture of multiple cells (Fig. 1a). Thus, cell-type-specific effects (the parameter vectors βt as defined above) must be resolved from aggregate spot-level readouts. To derive a spot-level model from equation (1), we assume that the spatial niche encodings Xi are the same for all cells of the same type within each spot; thus, we denote the spot-specific and cell-type-specific covariate matrix as Xt,s (in many cases, we can assume that they are shared by all cell types within each spot and, thus, can drop the subscript t). Then, we directly aggregate the single-cell model in equation (1) across the cells in each spot to yield the relation$$E\left[{Z}_{s}|X\right]=\mathop{\sum }\limits_{t=1}^{T}{C}_{s,t}{F}^{-1}\left({X}_{s,t}{\beta }_{t}\right),$$
(2)
where Cs,t is a measure of representation of cell type t in spot s, which can be estimated by spot deconvolution methods (Methods). We emphasize here that βt is a vector of dimension p. Model derivation, parameter estimation and inference are also provided in Methods.By this construction, the coefficient vectors βt in equation (2) have the same interpretation as in the single-cell model in equation (1). For example, when Y represents proportion spliced-in of an exon in isoform sequencing data, we would use the logit link function and βt,j could, thus, be interpreted as the increase in log odds of retaining the exon if a cell of type t is in spatial niche j. This interpretation holds whether we are in the single-cell model in equation (1) or in the spatial mixture model in equation (2). In other words, under the model in equation (2), we can interpret the estimated coefficients as if we observe single cells, even though our data are compositional (Fig. 1a). The model in equation (2) accommodates a broader range of modalities as compared to existing methods such as NicheDE7 and C-Side10, which are limited to count-based gene expression analysis.In practice, spotGLM integrates naturally into standard spatially barcoded omics analysis pipelines, as we illustrate later through applications. First, users should perform cell type deconvolution of spatial spots and set up their analysis through an appropriate encoding of the spatial neighborhood. The choice of spatial niche encoding should be guided by the biological question of interest, as we demonstrate later through examples. For large datasets (for example, Visium HD), we propose SPARROW (described next), a method for selecting a power-preserving subset of spots. SpotGLM can then used to estimate and test cell-type-specific associations of each feature (gene, isoform or transcription factor (TF) motif) with the spatial niche encoding. SpotGLM is decoupled from the underlying deconvolution and niche encoding steps and is designed to integrate modularly into existing spatial analysis workflows.SPARROW: data distillation for power-preserving bounded-runtime analysisSpatial omics technologies can now profile hundreds of thousands to millions of cells or spots within a single experiment. However, as dataset sizes increase, feature association testing becomes computationally demanding, often requiring days to weeks of runtime. This motivates the need for principled data distillation strategies that preserve statistical power while controlling computational cost.To design such a strategy, we need to first ask what large spatial datasets provide. Increasing the number of observations (that is, spots or cells) reduces standard errors and improves statistical power for detecting small effect sizes. However, in practice, we are not interested in detecting arbitrarily small effects, which are likely not biologically interesting. Beyond a certain sample size, statistical power for effect sizes of practical interest saturates. Then, what do we gain from large data? The value of large spatial omics datasets lies instead in their ability to capture rare cell types and rare niche configurations with sufficient representation. These rare configurations are often undersampled in smaller datasets yet may be where critical biological insights reside. Large spatial omics datasets power the testing of hypotheses involving low-abundance cell states or rare disease-specific microenvironments.Traditional downsampling methods, such as random subsampling, discards rare but biologically relevant configurations while oversampling common configurations. Geometric sketching8 tries to address this problem but is sensitive to outliers and noise. Rasterization reduces data to lower resolution, which can be helpful in reducing data sparsity but may blur rare cell states and short-range interactions. Unlike these existing methods, SPARROW optimizes subset selection relative to the analysis at hand, as represented by the niche context matrix X. Specifically, SPARROW selects a subset of spots that maximizes power for testing the null hypothesis βt,j = 0 across all coefficients βt,j in the model in equation (2). This ensures that both common and rare configurations in the model matrix X remain well represented (Fig. 1b); thus, high power is maintained in the subsample for signal detection across all configurations.Here, we provide an intuitive introduction to SPARROW, with full derivation and algorithmic details given in Methods. Consider first the simplest case of a multiple regression \({Y}_{n\times 1}\sim {X}_{n\times p}{\beta }_{p\times 1}\), where our goal is to select a subset S of size K among \(\{1,2,\ldots ,n\}\) that retains maximal power for downstream testing of the parameters β. The power for testing \({\beta }_{j}\ne 0\) versus the null hypothesis \({\beta }_{j}=0\) is inversely proportional to the standard error in the estimation of βj. For a subsample S of spots, the sum of squared standard errors of the maximum likelihood estimate of \({\beta }_{p\times 1}\) is equal to the trace of the inverse Fisher information matrix \(f(S)={\rm{tr}}[{({X}_{S}^{{{\top }}}{X}_{S})}^{-1}]\) (Fig. 1c). This is the classical A-optimal design criterion. We use it as the default SPARROW objective because it directly targets the marginal variances of the regression coefficients, which are the quantities entering coefficient-wise Wald tests and the power retention stopping rule below. Thus, we choose S by minimizing the function f(S),$${S}^{\star }=\mathop{{{\arg }}\,\min }\limits_{S:|S|=K}f\left(S\right).$$
(3)
To extend the above logic to the GLM in equation (1) and SpotGLM in equation (2), note that the covariance matrix in GLMs follows the form (XTWX)−1 where W is a diagonal weight matrix that can be explicitly computed given the data. In SpotGLM, the covariance matrix must further account for cell type mixing within spatial spots but can still be explicitly and efficiently computed (Methods and Supplementary Notes 1 and 2). Hence, we can use the optimization criterion in equation (3) for GLM and SpotGLM.Because of the combinatorial search space across subsets of size K, an exhaustive search for the A-optimal subset in equation (3) is computationally intractable for large datasets. SPARROW therefore uses a stochastic greedy design algorithm: starting from an initial regularized information matrix, it iteratively adds the data point that most reduces \({\rm{tr}}\{I{(S)}^{-1}\}\), where I(S) is the plug-in Fisher information for the selected subset. This A-optimal objective is monotone and directly interpretable as reducing the sum of marginal coefficient variances, although it is not generally submodular for arbitrary multivariate designs. For theoretical reference, a regularized D-optimal variant maximizing \({\rm{logdet}}\left\{\varLambda +I\left(S\right)\right\}-{\rm{logdet}}\left(\varLambda \right)\) is monotone submodular and admits the standard greedy approximation guarantee. In practice, the A-optimal and D-optimal variants showed similar performance across benchmarks (Supplementary Fig. 1) and we use A-optimality by default because of its direct connection to coefficient-wise standard errors and power.SPARROW data distillation maintains high power for diverse downstream tasksFirst, we evaluated the performance of SPARROW on four large-scale spatial transcriptomic datasets, performing diverse downstream analyses. For each analysis, we compared SPARROW to existing data reduction methods (random selection, geometric sketching8 and rasterization9) using results obtained from the full dataset as the gold standard. Power was measured by recall, computed as the proportion of signals recovered in the subsampled data relative to those identified in the full dataset, stratified by signal strength as measured by the log false discovery q value in the full data (Fig. 2a). We focus on recall because data reduction primarily affects statistical power rather than error control; subsampling reduces sensitivity by decreasing effective sample size, while the calibration of false discoveries is governed by the downstream statistical method. Specificity curves, shown in Supplementary Fig. 2, are comparable across methods. Hence, recall provides the most direct measure of how well biological signal is preserved under data distillation.Fig. 2: SPARROW enables power-preserving data distillation across diverse spatial transcriptomic analyses.Full size imagea, Benchmarking recall (y axis) versus signal strength (x axis) across four spatial transcriptomics datasets demonstrates that SPARROW outperforms existing data reduction methods—including random sampling, geometric sketching and rasterization—across all settings. Each analysis uses results from the full dataset as the gold standard. b, In MERFISH CRC data, SPARROW selects a balanced subset of cells across all cell types, avoiding the power saturation in tumor cells seen in other methods. c, Spatial locations of tumor cells in the full MERFISH CRC dataset and in subsets obtained by random selection, geometric sketching and SPARROW, colored by annotated spatial niche. SPARROW retains tumor cells from all five niches, including rare niche configurations. d, Quantification of the tumor-cell niche composition shown in c, displaying the proportion of tumor cells from each annotated niche for the full dataset and for each data reduction method; numbers above the bars indicate cell counts. For the rarest configuration, Niche 3, SPARROW reaches sampling saturation: all tumor cells observed in the full dataset are retained in the selected subset. e, SPARROW’s performance on simulated data ranging from 10,000 to 5 million data points. Left: statistical power relative to full-data analysis. Middle: number of spots selected by SPARROW (y axis) as a function of full-data size (x axis). Right: runtime comparison between SPARROW and full-data analysis.As Sparrow can be applied to both cell-level and spot-level spatial data, for benchmarking, we included both data types: MERFISH, where each observational unit is a cell, and 10x Visium HD, where each observational unit is a spot (or grid point). The datasets used are described in detail in Methods. Each task in our benchmark relies on a different encoding of spatial covariates, derived from anatomical domains or from cell–cell interactions, resulting in distinct covariate matrices used by SPARROW to determine the optimal subset. This demonstrates how SPARROW can tailor data distillation to the analysis at hand, where covariates can be discrete or continuous.Below, we summarize the four benchmark tasks and results. Details of the models and hypotheses tested are given in Methods. Note that all analyses here are linear in the number of spots; thus, a 10% reduction by SPARROW equates to a 10× speed-up. As data size (in terms of the number of spots) grows, we expect the number of spots in the distilled data to plateau, leading to bounded runtime, as we demonstrate in a simulation at the end.Our first example uses a MERFISH CRC dataset, profiling 500 genes across 750,000 cells and five annotated regions11. Cells were assigned to 15 cell types. In this starting example, for illustration, we performed the simplest analysis; we used region labels as covariates and screened for region-specific differential expression within each cell type. For signals identified at 5% false discovery rate in the full data, SPARROW achieved over 90% recall using only 10% of the data, while other subsampling methods achieved less than 70% recall at the same sampling rate (Fig. 2a). Across varying data retention levels, SPARROW consistently achieved the highest recall (Supplementary Fig. 3). Note that rasterization and geometric sketching failed to recover some of the most significant signals identified in the full dataset.To understand why SPARROW achieves such high recall, we examined the subsample composition. While random and geometric sketching-based methods heavily sampled tumor cells, SPARROW selected a balanced representation across all (cell type, region) combinations (Fig. 2b). As shown in Fig. 2c,d, SPARROW captured tumor cells from all regions, including all tumor cells from niche 3, which was extremely rare. In contrast, random and sketching-based methods largely missed the rare configurations.Thus, when covariates are categorical (for example, cell type × region with one-hot encoding), SPARROW can be approximated by stratified sampling, both aiming to achieve balanced representation across groups. However, stratified sampling cannot be applied to analyses that involve mixture-based spot measurements or continuous covariates (such as local neighborhood cell type density or spatial gradients). In contrast, SPARROW operates directly on the model matrix and optimizes a power-based objective, allowing principled subset selection across categorical and continuous designs.The case of a continuous niche covariate is demonstrated in our second example, which uses Visium HD CRC data with 300,000 spots and eight deconvolved cell types. Here, we encoded the spatial niche of each spot as the average cell type composition across all spots within a distance of 64 μm. We used SpotGLM to identify genes with cell-type-specific niche dependence, with the negative binomial model and cell type composition as the covariate (Methods). As shown in Fig. 2a, SPARROW achieves >95% recall for strong signals and >80% recall for weak signals with just 20% of the data, outperforming all baseline methods. This example illustrates the capacity of SPARROW to handle continuous covariates and spot-level measurements.The third example uses a Xenium liver dataset with 200,000 cells12; we again used cell type composition as the niche encoding, as in the Visium HD analysis, but now included a baseline cell type (hepatocytes) to identify relative expression differences (Methods). This reflects a common analysis setup where the goal is to identify differential niche dependency relative to a dominant or reference population. The resulting model tested 5,600 hypotheses. Figure 2a shows that, with around 33% of the data, SPARROW achieves ≥99% recall for strong signals and nearly 80% recall even for borderline signals, while other methods have recall around 60% at the same data reduction.Lastly, our fourth example evaluated SPARROW on a public Visium HD kidney data for cell-type-specific spatially variable gene (SVG) analysis using CELINA13. This dataset contains 400,000 spots, which we rasterized to 100,000 spots to overcome extreme data sparsity. Unlike previous analyses, CELINA relies on a spatial kernel matrix rather than an explicit covariate matrix. To apply SPARROW, we performed a low-rank decomposition of the kernel and used the top components in the low-rank embedding as the covariate matrix X. As CELINA is run separately for each cell type, we also applied SPARROW separately per cell type. As shown in Fig. 2a, using only 15% of the data for each cell type, SPARROW achieved near-perfect recall, while baseline methods remained under 75% recall. This demonstrates SPARROW’s application beyond regression-based analyses to an exploratory analysis based on a spatial kernel matrix.As subsampling primarily affects statistical power, our focus has been on recall. Now, we verify that data reduction does not inflate false discoveries. Because true negatives are unknown in real data, we define precision and specificity relative to discoveries in the full dataset as an empirical reference. Supplementary Fig. 2 shows that all methods including SPARROW maintain high precision and specificity.Bounded runtime of SPARROWThe size of spatial omic datasets is rapidly increasing and reaching millions of data points per experiment. To illustrate the bounded runtime of SPARROW, we performed a simulation study designed to quantify how many data points are required to retain near-full statistical power as dataset size grows. Specifically, we simulated datasets ranging from 10,000 to 5 million observations and measured the subsample size needed to retain 97.5% of the power of the full dataset for detecting biological signals above a minimal effect size threshold.As shown in Fig. 2e, the power of the subsample exhibits two distinct regimes. In the first regime, when the full dataset itself is insufficient to detect effects of the target magnitude, SPARROW selects a constant fraction of the data (~55% for the specific simulation), reflecting the fact that power remains limited by sample size. In the second regime, beyond 500,000 observations in this simulation, saturation is reached by the full data for the targeted effect sizes. Beyond this point, SPARROW is able to select a decreasing number of optimally chosen data points while still guaranteeing power across all covariate configurations. Notably, while the runtime of full-data analysis grows linearly, SPARROW’s runtime plateaus and then decreases once we reach the saturated regime, maintaining nearly identical power with bounded runtime (Fig. 2e). We also show power and runtime at log scale (Supplementary Fig. 4). This demonstrates how SPARROW enables bounded-runtime inference as spatial omics datasets become increasingly large.SpotGLM enables accurate and scalable cell-type-specific niche differential testingAlthough SpotGLM is designed to generalize beyond count-based RNA data, we first evaluated its performance in the canonical RNA spatial transcriptomics setting. We generated spot-by-gene counts from a Poisson distribution under a predefined mixture model (Methods). In this framework, true cell-type-specific and niche-associated coefficients were known, enabling direct comparison between estimated and ground-truth parameters.We benchmarked SpotGLM against existing approaches for cell-type-specific spatial differential analysis, including C-SIDE10, NicheDE7, spVC14 and a commonly used baseline that assigns each spot to its dominant cell type and performs differential testing without modeling mixture proportions. For spVC, which does not explicitly parameterize cell-type-specific niche effects, we augmented the design matrix with cell type proportions and their interactions with niche covariates to approximate a cell-type-level analysis. Details of this benchmark are in Supplementary Information.Across increasing sample sizes, methods that explicitly model cell-type-specific niche effects achieved low estimation error and high statistical power (Supplementary Fig. 5). In contrast, the dominant-cell baseline exhibited substantially inflated type I error and biased coefficient estimates, demonstrating that ignoring cell mixing leads to spurious differential expression. spVC showed reduced accuracy and substantially higher computational cost in this setting.When paired with SPARROW, SpotGLM scaled efficiently with increasing data size, enabling large-scale analyses that are computationally infeasible for existing methods. While statistical performance in moderate-scale RNA settings was comparable across mixture-aware methods, SpotGLM integrates naturally with a power-preserving subsampling framework that maintains statistical calibration while achieving bounded runtime.Resolving niche-dependent fibroblast programs from spot-level mixtures in colorectal cancerWe first demonstrate SpotGLM and SPARROW in the context of spatial niche differential expression analysis using two Visium HD CRC datasets15. These datasets contain approximately 300,000 spatially barcoded spots with nine annotated cell types. Because of the substantial computational cost of full-data analysis, we applied SPARROW to distill the dataset to 75,000 spots and applied SpotGLM on this reduced dataset. Our objective is to identify niche-specific transcriptional programs within fibroblasts, which are key participants of extracellular matrix remodeling, immune modulation and tumor progression16,17.To evaluate whether SpotGLM can resolve cell-type-specific niche effects from such mixture-based data, we leveraged serial adjacent tissue sections profiled using Xenium human immuno-oncology profiling panel18 (Fig. 3a). Xenium provides true single-cell spatial transcriptomics data without mixture confounding; thus, this serial-slice design enables direct comparison of estimated niche-effect coefficients across modalities. However, Xenium profiles only a targeted panel of 380 genes, not the entire transcriptome. Thus, we focus on the intersection of genes available in both the Xenium panel and the Visium HD dataset.Fig. 3: SpotGLM coupled with SPARROW identify cell-type-specific gene expression changes in tumor-associated niches.Full size imagea, Schematic workflow of Visium HD and Xenium cross-platform validation. Right: GSEA pathway enrichment of top upregulated fibroblast genes associated with T cell niche in participant 1.Specifically, we first quantified the spatial niche for each Visium HD spot and each Xenium cell. In Visium HD, the niche was defined by averaging deconvolved cell type proportions within a 100-µm radius surrounding each spot. In Xenium, the niche was defined analogously using directly observed cell type identities within the same radius. For each gene, we then estimated its association with the neighborhood abundance of specific cell types, after adjusting for other neighborhood cell types. In Visium HD, we applied SpotGLM under a negative binomial model; for Xenium, in the absence of mixtures, we applied a standard negative binomial GLM (Fig. 3a).To ensure a meaningful cross-platform comparison, we imposed two criteria. First, we restricted analysis to niche cell types whose spatial distributions were reproducible across Xenium and Visium. Second, within each data modality, we verified that distinct niche effects remained statistically separable, thereby ensuring adequate discriminatory power for coefficient estimation. These criteria identified three robust niche cell types (tumor, T cells and B cells) on which subsequent analyses focused. We then directly compared fibroblast niche-effect coefficients, estimated for these cell types, from Visium HD SpotGLM versus those from Xenium single-cell GLM (Fig. 3a).Despite the differences in platform technology, we observed strong concordance between the SpotGLM coefficients estimated from Visium HD and the GLM coefficients estimated from Xenium. Spearman correlation coefficients of the estimated niche-effect sizes were high across participants. For tumor niche effects, correlations were 0.79 and 0.80 in participants 1 and 2, respectively (Fig. 3b,d). For T cell niche effects, correlations were 0.80 and 0.86 in participants 1 and 2, respectively (Fig. 3b,d). For B cell niche effects, correlations were slightly lower at 0.61 and 0.88 in participants 1 and 2, respectively (Supplementary Fig. 6). This coefficient-level agreement across serial tissue sections demonstrates that SpotGLM accurately recovers cell-type-specific niche effects from spot-level mixture measurements.To further contextualize these findings, we compared our tumor-associated and immune-associated fibroblast gene sets with recently defined cancer-associated fibroblast (CAF) subtypes identified using single-cell spatial transcriptomics across multiple cancer types19. We observed statistically significant enrichment of our tumor niche genes within tumor-associated CAF subtype signatures and enrichment of immune niche genes within CAF-immune subtype markers across both CRC participants (Fig. 3c,e). Given the known plasticity and interindividual variability of CAF programs, this concordance supports the biological validity of SpotGLM-derived niche signatures.Beyond methodological validation, SpotGLM identified distinct fibroblast transcriptional programs associated with tumor and immune niches. In this analysis, we modeled gene expression using a spot-level negative binomial GLM (Methods). We discovered that fibroblasts near tumor niches exhibit elevated expression of COL11A1, COL5A1 and COL4A1, which overlap with established tumor-associated CAF subtype markers19,20,21. Additional genes identified included COL1A1, COL3A1 and SPARC. SPARC has been shown to induce COL1A1 and COL3A1 expression in CRC-associated fibroblasts22 and COL1A1 serves as a sensitive and specific CAF marker associated with poor prognosis across multiple cancer types23,24. Pathway enrichment analysis confirmed that collagen organization and extracellular matrix remodeling were dominant biological processes (Fig. 3f), consistent with the known biology of CAF-mediated tumor progression25,26.In contrast, fibroblasts in T cell-dense niches showed enrichment of inflammatory programs, including CCL19 (Fig. 3g). CCL19-producing fibroblasts are also shown to promote tertiary lymphoid structure formation27. Pathway enrichment analysis of T cell niche fibroblast genes revealed significant enrichment of TNF signaling and cytokine-mediated signaling pathways (Fig. 3g), highlighting a niche-dependent inflammatory fibroblast state that may contribute to localized immune organization.The scale of whole-transcriptome Visium HD datasets presents substantial computational challenges for existing spatial differential expression methods. Direct full-resolution analysis of 300,000 spots per sample was computationally impractical under high-memory cloud configurations. In contrast, pairing SpotGLM with SPARROW enabled power-preserving subsampling (~75,000 spots) and completion of the analysis within practical runtime while maintaining concordance with full-data results.Continuous osmolarity gradient modeling reveals spatially structured fibroblast programs in mouse kidneyWe next applied SpotGLM to a Visium HD dataset of healthy adult mouse kidney28, in which the spatial niche was defined by osmolarity level and anatomic zone. Osmolarity is a fundamental determinant of kidney physiology, reflecting the kidney’s role in maintaining systemic water and electrolyte homeostasis. Along the corticomedullary axis, osmolarity increases progressively from the cortex to the papilla. As these technologies evolve toward high-resolution and multimodal profiling, statistical frameworks must address two emerging challenges: mixture confounding at spot resolution and computational scalability at increasing data volumes. In this work, we introduce spotGLM, a mixture-aware GLM framework for cell-type-specific differential testing across spatial modalities, together with SPARROW, a power-preserving submodular data selection strategy for scalable inference.SpotGLM extends the GLM to spatial data where each spatial coordinate can contain compositional mixtures of multiple cell types. By explicitly modeling modality-specific sampling noise and spatial mixing, SpotGLM enables hypothesis testing across a wide range of omics modalities, including gene expression, chromatin accessibility and RNA splicing. Through simulations and real-data applications, we demonstrate accurate recovery of cell-type-specific niche effects under mixture, including differential gene expression, spatial isoform switching and regulatory motif accessibility.The biological applications presented here also yield findings beyond methodological validation. In CRC, serial-slice cross-platform comparison between Visium HD and Xenium provided a stringent test of mixture-aware inference, demonstrating coefficient-level concordance of fibroblast niche effects across technologies. This validation establishes that spotGLM can recover cell-type-specific niche programs from spot-level whole-transcriptome data with accuracy comparable to single-cell-resolved measurements. In mouse kidney, modeling a continuous corticomedullary osmolarity gradient revealed fibroblast transcriptional programs associated with increasing osmotic stress that are not captured by coarse anatomical region labels. In spatial long-read data, spotGLM enabled cell-type-resolved analysis of spatial isoform switching, clarifying fundamental distinctions between global isoform changes and within-cell-type splicing regulation. Lastly, in spatial ATAC-seq of mouse brain, mixture-aware modeling uncovered oligodendrocyte-specific regulatory motif enrichment across brain regions, extending spatial differential testing to chromatin-level regulatory programs. Together, these examples illustrate how mixture-aware modeling enables discovery of spatially structured, cell-type-specific molecular programs across modalities.Complementing spotGLM, SPARROW addresses the computational bottleneck posed by large spatial datasets while reflecting a broader statistical insight. As spatial technologies scale to hundreds of thousands or millions of observations per experiment, statistical power for detecting biologically meaningful effect sizes eventually saturates; beyond a certain sample size, additional observations primarily reduce standard errors for increasingly small effects that may be of limited practical relevance. The true advantage of large spatial datasets lies instead in their ability to capture rare cell types and rare niche configurations with sufficient representation. SPARROW leverages an A-optimality-based proxy for statistical power, selecting subsets that preserve information across covariate configurations, including rare ones. As a result, the number of observations required for inference can plateau even as total dataset size continues to grow, yielding bounded-runtime analysis without sacrificing sensitivity for effect sizes of interest. This regime is increasingly important as next-generation spatial omics platforms routinely generate millions of spatial measurements per sample, shifting the statistical challenge from sample scarcity to configuration coverage.While our framework provides a scalable and flexible foundation for spatial analysis, several caveats merit discussion. As long as the user chooses a large enough starting value for \({\lambda }_{0}\), the parameter fitting of the SpotGLM should converge.SPARROW formulation and algorithmic detailsFormulation of SPARROW objectiveOur data consist of responses \({Y}_{n\times 1}\) and covariates \({X}_{n\times p}\), where n is the number of data points and p is the number of covariates. Our analyses assume that \({Y}_{i}{\rm{| }}{X}_{i}\) follows a mixture-aware GLM of the form in equation (2). Let \(\beta\) be the coefficients for this model, where \({\beta }_{t,j}\) measures the effect of the jth covariate on Y in cell type t. To simplify ensuing notation, we flatten \(\beta\) and refer to each of its elements as \({\beta }_{j}\). We use the term ‘data point’ rather than ‘cell’ or ‘spot’ to stress that SPARROW is applicable to both cell-level and spot-level data (for cell-level data, we would simply replace the generalized mixed linear model with a standard GLM). (8)
where c, the power retention threshold, is close to 1. To achieve this, we first fix the subset size K and identify the subset \({S}_{K}^{\star }\) with criterion$${S}_{K}^{\star }=\mathop{\min }\limits_{S:|S|=K}f\left(S\right),$$
(9)
where$$f(S)={\rm{tr}}{\left({X}_{S}^{{{\top }}}W{X}_{S}\right)}^{-1},$$
(10)
and W is a diagonal matrix that depends on the specific model used in the analysis. The explicit form of W for different models is derived in Supplementary Notes 1 and 2. The criterion in equation (10) is the A-optimal design criterion. As \({X}_{S}^{{{\top }}}W{X}_{S}\) is the Fisher information matrix, f(S) is the sum of the asymptotic marginal variances of the coefficient estimates. We use this criterion because the marginal standard errors directly determine power for coefficient-wise Wald tests.Greedy optimization of the A-optimal subsetThe optimization in equation (9) is a cardinality-constrained A-optimal design problem. Because exhaustive search is infeasible, SPARROW uses a stochastic greedy algorithm. Let \({M}_{S}={\Lambda }+{Z}_{S}^{{\top }}{Z}_{S}\), where \(Z={W}^{1/2}X\) and \(\Lambda \succ 0\) is a small ridge term or initial information matrix. At each iteration, SPARROW samples a candidate batch from the unselected observations and adds the candidate u that minimizes \({\rm{tr}}\{{M}_{S\cup \{u\}}^{-1}\}\). The ridge term ensures that the inverse is well defined even at early iterations.The A-optimal objective is monotone; adding observations can only increase the information matrix and, therefore, can only decrease \({\rm{tr}}({M}_{S}^{-1})\). To determine the suitable subsample size \({K}^{\star }\), we perform an approximate power calculation. The power of the Wald tests for testing \({H}_{0}:{\beta }_{j}=0\) when the standard error is \(\sigma\) and the true value is \({\beta }_{j}=b > 0\) can be approximated under asymptotic normality by$${P}_{\text{theory}}\left(\sigma ,b\right)=1-\varPhi \left({z}_{1-{\alpha }/{2}}-\frac{b}{\sigma }\right)-\varPhi \left(-{z}_{1-\alpha /2}-\frac{b}{\sigma }\right),$$
(11)
where \(\alpha\) is the level of the test and \({Z}_{1-\alpha }\) is the inverse cumulative distribution function of a standard normal evaluated at \(1-\alpha\). (12)
where c is what we call the ‘power retention ratio’. (13)

(14)
That is, the approximate standard error for the optimal subset \({S}_{K}^{* }\) must be lower than the target standard error for all covariates.The complete SPARROW algorithmIn the previous sections, we introduced how SPARROW uses greedy selection to iteratively add data points to the subsample to maximize the statistical power of downstream analyses. We also introduced a natural stopping criterion to achieve a specified proportion of the power attainable with the complete dataset. Integrating these ideas, we now describe in detail the SPARROW algorithm.We start by scaling each column j of \(Z={W}^{1/2}X\) by the corresponding target standard error \({{\rm{SE}}}_{\text{target},j}\). After scaling, a standard error ≤ 1 would indicate that the target precision in the estimation of the coefficient has been attained by the data subsample:$${\mathrm{SE}}\left({\hat{\beta }}_{S,j}\right)\le 1\,{\text{for}}\, {\rm{all}}\,j.$$
(15)
When, for a coefficient j, the above criterion is achieved for a subset S, we say that the coefficient has converged.We start with a data subsample of S = ∅. In each iteration, the algorithm greedily selects the data point i that minimizes$${\rm{trace}}\left[{({Z}_{S\cup \{i\}}^{{\top }}{Z}_{S\cup \{i\}})}^{-1}\right]$$
(16)
and set S←S∪i. where d(i, cortex boundary) denotes the Euclidean distance from spot i to the nearest cortex boundary spot and d(i, papilla boundary) denotes the distance to the nearest papilla boundary spot. This formulation yields \({O}_{i}\in [0,1]\), where values approaching 1 indicate proximity to the papilla (high osmolarity) and values approaching 0 indicate proximity to the cortex (low osmolarity), consistent with the physiological osmolality gradient of the mammalian kidney.The Xenium kidney tissue section exhibited a radial anatomical organization, with the papilla located centrally and the cortex at the periphery. To construct an osmolarity proxy, we identified a reference cell located within the inner papilla region as the central anchor point. For each cell i, we computed the osmolarity proxy \({O}_{i}\) on the basis of its radial position:$${O}_{i}=1-\frac{d\left(i,\text{papilla center}\right)}{R}$$
(19)
where d(i, papilla center) denotes the Euclidean distance from cell i to the papilla reference cell and \(R\) denotes the radius of the tissue section (that is, the maximum distance from the papilla center to the tissue boundary). This formulation yields \({O}_{i}\in [0,1]\), where values approaching 1 indicate proximity to the papilla center (high osmolarity) and values approaching 0 indicate proximity to the cortical periphery (low osmolarity).Visium HD kidney SpotGLM model setup and analysisTo enable efficient analysis while preserving statistical power, we applied SPARROW to select 70,000 representative spots and subsequently fit SpotGLM to both the full and subsampled datasets. Analysis of the full data required approximately 5.7 days of computation and analysis of the subsampled data required approximately 18.7 h of computation. We modeled gene expression using a spot-level negative binomial GLM: \({Z}_{s,g}\sim \text{NB}\left({\mu }_{s,g},{\gamma }_{g}\right),\,{\mu }_{s,g}=\sum _{t}{\pi }_{s,t}\exp ({X}_{s,\text{pap}}{\beta }_{t,\,\text{papilla}}^{g}+{X}_{s,\text{cor}}{\beta }_{t,\,\text{cortex}}^{g}\)\(+{O}_{s}{\beta }_{t,\,\text{osmolarity}}^{g}+\log {L}_{s}).\). Here, \({Z}_{s,g}\) is the count for gene g in spot s, \({\pi }_{s,t}\) is the proportion of cell type t in spot s and corresponds to the \({C}_{s,t}\) in the SpotGLM model, \({X}_{s}\) is a one-hot-encoded matrix consisting of the region identity of each spot, \({O}_{s}\) is the continuous osmolarity gradient at spot s and \({L}_{s}\) is the library size of spot s. The parameters of interest are \({\beta }_{t,\,\text{osmolarity}}^{g}\), the gene-specific osmolarity-effect on cell type t. This model is also used to compare fitted coefficients of Xenium and Visium HD mouse kidney data. We test the null hypothesis using Wald tests \({H}_{0}:{\beta }_{t,\text{osmolarity}}^{g}=0.\) If \({\beta }_{t,\text{osmolarity}}^{g}\ne 0\), then the osmolarity level influences the gene expression of gene g in cell type t.Xenium kidney standard GLM model setup and analysisAs Xenium measures single cells and not mixtures of cells, we modeled gene expression using a standard negative binomial GLM: \({Y}_{c,g}|c\in \text{type}T\sim \text{NB}\left({\mu }_{c,g},{\gamma }_{g}\right),\,{\mu }_{c,g}=\exp ({X}_{c,\text{pap}}{\beta }_{T,\,\text{papilla}}^{g}+{X}_{c,\text{cor}}{\beta }_{T,\,\text{cortex}}^{g}\)\(+{O}_{c}{\beta }_{T,\,\text{osmolarity}}^{g}+\log {L}_{c})\). Here, \({Y}_{c,g}\) is the count for gene g in cell c, \({X}_{c}\) is a one-hot-encoded matrix consisting of the region identity of each cell, \({O}_{c}\) is the continuous osmolarity gradient for cell c and \({L}_{c}\) is the library size of cell c. The parameters of interest are \({\beta }_{T,\,\text{osmolarity}}^{g}\), the gene-specific osmolarity-effect on cell type T. We test the null hypothesis using Wald tests \({H}_{0}:{\beta }_{T,\text{osmolarity}}^{g}=0\). If \({\beta }_{T,\text{osmolarity}}^{g}\ne 0\), then the osmolarity level influences the gene expression of gene g in a specific cell type T.Spatial isoform switching analysis in mouse olfactory bulbThis dataset, generated and analyzed by Lebrigand et al.5, contains spatial long read of adult C57BL/6 mice olfactory bulbs aged over 2 months, includes 74 million long reads, filtered to retain only UMIs that fully span all exon–exon junctions for their mapped isoform. After filtering, 2.19 million UMIs with unambiguous transcript structure were retained, spanning 918 spatial spots, with a mean of 1,917 UMIs and a median of 974 isoforms per spot. In total, 23,560 Gencode reference isoforms from 13,291 genes were detected.For gene g, assume for simplicity that there are two splice variants (isoform 1 versus isoform 2). Let the true relative proportion of isoform 1 in spot s be \({\gamma }_{s}^{g}\). This spot-level quantity \({\gamma }_{s}^{g}\) is a weighted average of the cell-specific isoform relative proportions across the cells that make up spot s, weighted by each cell’s total expression of gene g. Aggregating across cells in spot s of the same type, we have \({\gamma }_{s,g}=\frac{{\sum }_{i\in s}{\gamma }_{i,g{\mu }_{{T}_{i},g}}}{{\sum }_{i\in s}{\mu }_{{T}_{i},g}}=\frac{{\sum }_{t}{\gamma }_{t,g}{\pi }_{s,t}\,{\mu }_{t,g}}{{\sum }_{t}{\pi }_{s,t}{\mu }_{t,g}}\).At the single-cell level, we use logistic regression to model the dependence of splicing (isoform 1 versus isoform 2) on the spatial niche X, which, for the mouse olfactory bulb data, is simply the one-hot-encoded region for each cell. We assume that this dependence is cell type specific. That is, we assume \({Y}_{i,g}\sim \text{Bin}\left({n}_{i,g},{\gamma }_{{T}_{i},g}\right)\)\(,\,\text{logit}\left({\gamma }_{{T}_{i},g}\right)=X{\beta }_{{T}_{i},g}\), where \({Y}_{i,g}\) represents the number of reads mapping to isoform 1 for gene g in cell i, \({n}_{i,g}\) represents the total number of reads mapping to gene g, \({\beta }_{t,g}\) is a vector \(({\beta }_{t,g,r}:r=1,\ldots ,R)\), representing the increase in log odds of a read belonging to isoform 1, for type t cells if they lie in region r. The equivalent spot-level model is \({Y}_{s,g}\sim \text{Bin}({n}_{s,g},{p}_{s,g}),\,{p}_{s,g}=\sum _{t}{w}_{s,g,t}{\text{Logit}}^{-1}({X}_{s}{\beta }_{t,g}),\,{w}_{s,g,t}=\frac{{\pi }_{s,t}{\mu }_{g,t}}{{\sum }_{{t}^{{\prime} }}{\pi }_{s,{t}^{{\prime} }}{\mu }_{g,{t}^{{\prime} }}}\), where \({Y}_{s,g}\) is the count of isoform 1 of gene g in spot s, \({n}_{s,g}\) is the total expression of gene g in spot s, \({\pi }_{s,t}\) is the deconvolution proportion of cell type t in spot s and \({\mu }_{s,g,t}\) is the expected expression of gene g in cell type t in spot s. \({\mu }_{g,t}\) is estimated by the model \({Y}_{s,g}\sim \text{Pois}\left(\sum _{t}{\pi }_{s,t}{\mu }_{g,t}\right)\), which is equivalent to a SpotGLM with the covariate being solely an intercept vector.To detect cell-type-specific isoform switching between regions r and r′ in cell type t, we test the null hypothesis \({H}_{0}:{\beta }_{t,g,r}={\beta }_{t,g,{r}^{{\prime} }}\) using a Wald contrast test. Thus, for 11 cell types and five regions in the mouse olfactory bulb data, a maximum possible of \(11\times \left(\genfrac{}{}{0ex}{}{5}{2}\right)=110\) tests can be performed for each gene. For a region where the cell type t is not present or if the gene is adequately expressed in fewer than five spots, the test is not performed. A gene g is defined as being adequately expressed within a cell type t if the total estimated proportion of transcripts belonging to gene g in cell type t within spot s is greater than 1/50,000.P22 mouse brain spatial ATAC-seq analysisThis dataset contains 9,215 spots of dimension 50 µm × 50 µm. Each spot was assigned to one of 14 annotated spatial domains on the basis of their spatial location. For each spot, peaks were called of length 50 bp. Then, peaks were aggregated either by gene or by TF motif. When aggregated by gene, 24,027 genes were represented. When aggregated by TF motif, 746 motifs were represented. We model the motif score for each region as \({Y}_{s,m}\sim N\left(\sum _{t}{\pi }_{s,t}{X}_{s}{\beta }_{t},{\sigma }_{m}^{2}\right)\), where \({\pi }_{s,t}\) is the deconvolution proportion of cell type t in spot s, \({X}_{s}\) is the one-hot-encoded region membership for spot s, \({\sigma }_{m}^{2}\) is a motif specific variance and \({\beta }_{t}\) is the region coefficient vector for cell type t. The entry \({\beta }_{t,r}\) of the vector \({\beta }_{t}\) encodes the cell-type-specific enrichment of the given TF or gene for cells that reside in region r. To detect differential accessibility, we tested for region contrasts using a Wald contrast test,$${H}_{0}:{\beta}_{t,r,m}={\beta}_{t,{r}^{{\prime}}\!,m}\,\text{vs}\,{H}_{1}:{\beta}_{t,r,m}\ne {\beta}_{t,{r}^{{\prime}}\!,m}$$
(20)
Motifs for which the test above is rejected can be said to be marker motifs for region r in cell type t.Reporting summaryFurther information on research design is available in the Nature Portfolio Reporting Summary linked to this article.

Data availability

All datasets are publicly available. In spatial transcriptomics analysis, the Visium HD human CRC participant 1 and participant 2 data can be downloaded from the 10X genomics website (https://www.10xgenomics.com/products/visium-hd-spatial-gene-expression/dataset-human-crc). Xenium human CRC data can also be downloaded from the 10X genomics website (https://www.10xgenomics.com/platforms/visium/product-family/dataset-human-crc). The Visium HD mouse kidney data can also be downloaded from the 10X genomics website (https://www.10xgenomics.com/datasets/visium-hd-cytassist-gene-expression-libraries-of-mouse-kidney). Xenium mouse kidney data can be downloaded from Zenodo (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.12709329)55. Cell type deconvolution requires single-cell RNA-seq data as reference data. The matched CRC single-cell RNA-seq is available from the 10X website (https://www.10xgenomics.com/products/visium-hd-spatial-gene-expression/dataset-human-crc). The mouse kidney scRNA-seq atlas can be accessed online (https://cellxgene.cziscience.com/collections/92fde064-2fb4-41f8-b85c-c6904000b859). The MERFISH CRC data can be downloaded from the Vizgen website using the colon cancer 2 sample (https://info.vizgen.com/ffpe-showcase?submissionGuid=756dd605-23f2-4332-89d4-2cd4e0a5a33b). The Xenium data analysis used lung cancer xenium data available from the 10X genomics website (https://www.10xgenomics.com/datasets/human-liver-data-xenium-human-multi-tissue-and-cancer-panel-1-standard). In spatial isoform analysis, the isoform data are available from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) under accession code GSE153859. In spatial ATAC-seq analysis, the mouse brain spatial ATAC data are available from the GEO under accession code GSE205055. Specifically, we downloaded the fragment file of the mouse brain P22 replicate 2 ATAC sample for the analysis.

SPARROW code for data selection is available from GitHub (https://github.com/kaishumason/SPARROW). SpotGLM code is available from GitHub (https://github.com/kaishumason/SpotGLM). Tutorials and usage examples are available in the GitHub repositories.
